_about: Curated source map for quotes in reflections. Claude may only quote these works,
and the app (never Claude) builds every link from this file.
After editing, run:  uv run python tools/build_sources.py
That checks every link and downloads the texts used to verify quote wording.
To (re)build just some works:  uv run python tools/build_sources.py republic ethics_spinoza
Fields:
pages:  how the work is split into linkable pages on Wikisource. One of:
{'single': title}  the whole work is one page
{'template': title, 'levels': [...]}  {n} = number, {roman} = Roman
numeral; 'levels' gives the count at each level, or a list of
counts per parent (Discourses: 4 books, 30/26/26/13 chapters)
{'prefix': title, 'pattern': regex}  every subpage whose remaining
title matches the regex; its groups become the page's location
(Roman numerals and number words become numbers; 'aliases'
renames groups, e.g. a Summa part to 'I-II')
sections:  how passages inside a page are numbered, if the app can tell:
'numbered_paragraphs' (paragraphs start '3.'), 'roman_headings', or null
location_from_section:  show only the section number as the location
(for works numbered straight through, aphorism by aphorism)
note:   extra guidance for Claude about this work

apology.author: Plato
apology.title: Apology
apology.location_format: Stephanus number if you know it, e.g. 38a; otherwise leave empty
apology.note: Socrates' defence speech at his trial. Introduce quotes as Socrates speaking.

crito.author: Plato
crito.title: Crito
crito.location_format: Stephanus number if you know it, e.g. 49b; otherwise leave empty
crito.note: Socrates in prison, on justice and obligation. Introduce quotes as Socrates speaking.

phaedo.author: Plato
phaedo.title: Phaedo
phaedo.location_format: Stephanus number if you know it, e.g. 64a; otherwise leave empty
phaedo.note: Socrates' last day, on death and the soul.

symposium.author: Plato
symposium.title: Symposium
symposium.location_format: Stephanus number if you know it, e.g. 210a; otherwise leave empty
symposium.note: Speeches on love; Socrates recounts Diotima's teaching.

republic.author: Plato
republic.title: Republic
republic.location_format: book number, e.g. 7 (Stephanus numbers can follow: 7, 514a)

epicurus.author: Epicurus
epicurus.title: Letters and Principal Doctrines
epicurus.translation: Robert Drew Hicks (1925), preserved in Diogenes Laërtius, Lives, Book X
epicurus.work_page: Lives of the Eminent Philosophers/Book X

pages.single: Lives of the Eminent Philosophers/Book X

epicurus.note: Book X of Diogenes Laërtius' Lives: a short life of Epicurus, then his own Letters to Herodotus, Pythocles and Menoeceus (pleasure, desire, death) and his Principal Doctrines. Quote Epicurus' own words, from the letters or doctrines.

on_old_age.author: Cicero
on_old_age.title: On Old Age
on_old_age.note: A dialogue in which the elder Cato defends old age: on work, pleasure, memory and facing death calmly.

tusculan_disputations.author: Cicero
tusculan_disputations.title: Tusculan Disputations
tusculan_disputations.note: Five books: on the fear of death (1), bearing pain (2), grief (3), other disturbing emotions (4), and whether virtue is enough for a happy life (5).

confessions.author: Augustine
confessions.title: Confessions
confessions.work_page: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers: Series I/Volume I/Confessions

pages.prefix: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers: Series I/Volume I/Confessions/

consolation.author: Boethius
consolation.title: The Consolation of Philosophy
consolation.location_format: the section's title as printed, e.g. Fortune's Malice
consolation.note: Written in prison awaiting execution: Lady Philosophy consoles Boethius on lost fortune, false goods (wealth, fame, power, pleasure), true happiness, evil, and free will. Alternates prose and verse.

proslogium.author: Anselm of Canterbury
proslogium.title: Proslogium
proslogium.note: A prayerful meditation: 'faith seeking understanding' and 'I believe in order to understand' (chapter 1), and the argument for God as that than which nothing greater can be conceived.

summa.author: Thomas Aquinas
summa.title: Summa Theologiae
summa.translation: Fathers of the English Dominican Province (1917)
summa.location_format: part.question.article, e.g. I-II.2.8 (only the moral parts I-II and II-II are available)
summa.note: Quote the body of an article or a reply, not the objections, which state views Aquinas rejects.

pages.pattern: ^(First Part of the Second Part|Second Part of the Second Part)/Question (\d+)$

inferno.author: Dante Alighieri
inferno.title: Inferno
inferno.note: The first part of the Divine Comedy: lost 'midway upon the journey of our life', Dante descends through Hell, where each sin becomes its own punishment.

purgatorio.author: Dante Alighieri
purgatorio.title: Purgatorio
purgatorio.note: The climb up the mountain of Purgatory: change as slow, patient work; love misdirected, too weak, or excessive as the root of every fault (cantos 17-18).

paradiso.author: Dante Alighieri
paradiso.title: Paradiso
paradiso.note: The ascent through Heaven: contentment ('in His will is our peace', canto 3), and the love that moves the sun and the other stars.

pensees.author: Blaise Pascal
pensees.title: Pensées (Thoughts)
pensees.note: Only Sections I-III (thoughts 1-241) are available to quote: on the mind and style, the misery of man without God (diversion and restlessness: 'all the unhappiness of men arises from one single fact, that they cannot stay quietly in their own chamber', 139; vanity, habit, self-love), and the wager (233). Ideas from later sections, such as the heart having its reasons (277) or the thinking reed (347), may be paraphrased and attributed but not quoted.

ethics_spinoza.author: Baruch Spinoza
ethics_spinoza.title: Ethics
ethics_spinoza.location_format: part.proposition, e.g. 4.67 (add 'note' or 'appendix' if relevant: 3, definitions of the emotions)

kierkegaard_selections.note: Selections only: Diapsalmata (aphorisms of the restless 'aesthetic' life), The Banquet (from Stages on Life's Way), Fear and Trembling (abridged: Abraham and the leap of faith), and late religious writings. Quote only from these.
